article.headline: A Solo Dev Ships Google's Unreleased Code — and Finds a Flaw
article.lede: When researchers at Google published a new technique for compressing AI memory in April 2025, they released the mathematics and nothing else. Tom Turney, a developer in Texas, read the preprint, built an implementation inside llama.cpp, and shipped working code before Google did. The engineering story is real; the mythology that accumulated around it is shakier.
article.body:
The paper, “TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-Optimal Distortion Rate,” was posted to arXiv in April 2025 by researchers at **Alphabet** (GOOGL) and accepted at ICLR 2026. It addresses *KV cache* compression — the KV cache is the memory table that large language models build during inference from key-value attention pairs, growing linearly with context length and becoming the binding constraint on how long a conversation a model can sustain within a hardware budget. Google released no reference implementation alongside the paper.

Turney’s work, hosted on GitHub as turboquant_plus, integrates directly with *llama.cpp*, the community runtime that powers most local-LLM inference on consumer hardware. The viral posts credit the development to Claude — Anthropic’s AI coding assistant — though Turney’s own announcement emphasized technical results without that framing. The headline figures require unpacking: the 3.7× speed improvement compares Turney’s final optimized build (2,747 *tok/s* for prefill) to his own initial prototype (739 tok/s), both measured on an Apple M5 Max — an engineering-optimization story, not a comparison to anything Google produced. The 4.6× compression refers to the turbo3 tier: 3.5 bits per value versus a 16-bit float baseline, with roughly a 1% *perplexity* penalty on a standard text benchmark. The “35B model on a MacBook” result uses Qwen 3.5 35B, a *mixture-of-experts* architecture that is already unusually memory-efficient, on an M5 Max with 128 GB of unified memory.

TurboQuant composes two distinct algorithms. *PolarQuant* converts KV cache vectors into polar coordinates, applies a *Walsh-Hadamard Transform* rotation, and then runs Lloyd-Max scalar quantization — the rotation concentrates variance so that aggressive bit-reduction accumulates less error. *QJL* (Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform) was designed as a second stage, using a classic dimensionality-preserving random projection reduced to single sign bits to clean up residual error. Turney and at least five other independent teams found that QJL hurts rather than helps; his production pipeline drops the second stage entirely, relying on PolarQuant alone.

The viral framing — “solo dev reverse-engineered Google’s billion-dollar algorithm” — overstates the drama on two fronts. The paper was freely available on arXiv for nearly a year before Google’s March 2026 blog post triggered the wave of coverage, so Turney was implementing a public preprint, not cracking a proprietary system. The paper itself carries unresolved academic controversy: Jianyang Gao, lead author of *RaBitQ* at ETH Zurich, publicly accused the Google team of benchmarking RaBitQ on deliberately hobbled hardware — single-core CPU, multithreading disabled — while running TurboQuant on a **NVIDIA** (NVDA) A100 GPU, and of building on RaBitQ’s core random-rotation idea without adequate attribution. Gao filed a complaint with ICLR’s ethics committee. None of that diminishes Turney’s engineering contribution; it reframes the story as a skilled developer who built a useful open-source tool from a contested paper that its own authors declined to release.

concepts.definition: Short for key-value cache, the memory table a transformer model builds during inference by recording the key and value projections for every prior token. It grows linearly with context length and is typically the binding constraint on how large a context window a given hardware budget can sustain.

An open-source C++ inference engine created by Georgi Gerganov that allows large language models to run on consumer hardware — laptops, desktops, and phones — without requiring a dedicated GPU. It has become the de-facto runtime for local LLM experimentation and is the integration target for Turney’s implementation.

A quantization algorithm that converts high-dimensional vectors into polar coordinates, applies a Walsh-Hadamard Transform rotation to concentrate variance, and then compresses each coordinate using scalar quantization. The rotation step is key: it distributes variance more evenly, allowing fewer bits to represent the same information with less accumulated error.

A compression technique that applies a Johnson-Lindenstrauss random projection — a classical tool for preserving inter-point distances when mapping to lower dimensions — and then reduces the output to a single sign bit per value. Designed as TurboQuant’s second stage to clean up residual error, but found by multiple independent teams to degrade rather than improve practical performance.

A fast orthogonal linear transform that maps a vector into a basis of ±1 coefficients. In quantization, applying a randomized WHT rotation before compressing serves to spread energy evenly across all coordinates, reducing worst-case quantization error without requiring storage of the rotation matrix.

A neural network architecture containing many specialized sub-networks that routes each token through only a small subset of them at inference time. The result is a model with high total parameter count but low active memory pressure — making it more feasible to run on consumer hardware than a dense model of equivalent capacity.

A standard benchmark metric for language models measuring how well the model predicts a held-out text corpus — lower is better. A 1% perplexity increase from compression means the model finds text marginally less predictable than the uncompressed baseline, a degradation typically considered acceptable.

An optimal scalar quantization scheme that places discrete representation levels (centroids) to minimize mean squared error given the distribution of the input signal. In TurboQuant, it determines the finite set of values used to represent each rotated KV cache coordinate after the WHT step.

A vector quantization method developed at ETH Zurich that, like TurboQuant, applies a random orthogonal rotation before quantizing high-dimensional vectors. Its lead author filed an ethics complaint with ICLR alleging the TurboQuant paper benchmarked RaBitQ under deliberately degraded hardware conditions while presenting TurboQuant results from far superior hardware.

A standard throughput measure for language model inference counting how many output tokens — roughly word-fragments — the model produces per second. The figure meaningfully depends on whether it measures prefill speed (processing the input prompt) or decode speed (generating each output token), as the two have different computational profiles.

repos.summary: Tom Turney’s open-source implementation of Google’s TurboQuant KV cache compression algorithm, integrated into llama.cpp with Metal kernels for Apple Silicon. The first reproducible implementation of the ICLR 2026 paper, and its benchmarks revealed that the paper’s QJL stage degrades rather than improves practical performance. Three compression tiers — turbo4 (3.8×), turbo3 (4.6×), turbo2 (6.4×) — trade compression depth against perplexity cost.

article.fact_check: The 'reverse-engineered' framing is inaccurate: the TurboQuant paper was freely available on arXiv for nearly a year before Turney built his implementation — he implemented a public preprint, not a proprietary system. The 3.7× speed figure compares Turney’s final build to his own initial prototype, not to Google's results or an uncompressed baseline. The '35B on a MacBook' result requires 128 GB of unified memory (M5 Max) and a memory-efficient MoE architecture, so it does not generalize to typical laptop configurations. The underlying paper also carries unresolved misconduct allegations from the RaBitQ team regarding benchmarking methodology and attribution.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.

sources.title: Nancy Pelosi's 2026 Stock Moves — Motley Fool

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

poster_roundtablespace.blurb: RoundtableSpace is the X account for Mario Nawfal’s Roundtable, a leading crypto and macro-focused Twitter Spaces show hosted by Mario Nawfal. The account covers breaking crypto news, market analysis, memecoin trends, DeFi, and geopolitical events, often drawing hundreds of thousands of live listeners. With over 155,000 followers, it is one of the most prominent crypto discussion platforms on X.
poster_roundtablespace.credibility_note: The account is a degen/alpha-oriented crypto show; content is often speculative and promotional. No major corrections or controversies were found in the provided sources.
